title: Johnson & Johnson to acquire Ollin Biosciences in US$3.3B ophthalmology deal | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication
summary: The pharmaceutical company will pay US$2.2 billion upfront, with an additional US$1.125 billion tied to regulatory and commercial milestones.
thbAction: Use the article as an entry point to pitch THB's commercial visibility layer for territory planning, account prioritization, and next-best-action for pharma leadership teams.
contentHtml:
USA—Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to acquire ophthalmology drug developer Ollin Biosciences for up to US$3.3 billion to strengthen its eye disease portfolio and expand its presence in the wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) market.

The pharmaceutical company will pay US$2.2 billion upfront, with an additional US$1.125 billion tied to regulatory and commercial milestones.

Ollin’s lead candidate, OLN324, is an investigational bispecific antibody designed to target two biological pathways implicated in retinal diseases: vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiopoietin-2 (Ang2).

The drug is currently in Phase III development for wet AMD and diabetic macular oedema (DME), two major causes of vision loss.

Competition in the retinal disease market

The acquisition gives J&J access to a late-stage candidate targeting a market dominated by Regeneron’s and Bayer’s Eylea (aflibercept) and Roche’s Vabysmo (faricimab).

Both are established anti-VEGF therapies that generate substantial sales in retinal disease treatment.

However, increasing competition and patent expiry are reshaping the market.

Eylea is approaching the end of key patent protections, while biosimilar versions are entering the market, creating pressure on pricing and market share.

Ollin has positioned OLN324 as a potential competitor to existing treatments, citing results from a Phase Ib head-to-head study against Vabysmo.

The company reported greater improvements in visual acuity and retinal fluid reduction, alongside other clinical outcomes.

The candidate is advancing into Phase III trials for both wet AMD and DME.

J&J plans to continue its development and build on Ollin’s research as it seeks to strengthen its position in ophthalmology.

Commenting on the acquisition, Kip Connor, J&J’s ophthalmology disease area stronghold leader, said the clinical data generated so far were encouraging and indicated the potential for improved retinal fluid reduction and longer intervals between treatments.

These characteristics could reduce treatment frequency and improve convenience for patients.

Blackstone to finance Phase III development

Alongside the acquisition, J&J announced a separate funding agreement with Blackstone Life Sciences.

The investment firm will provide US$750m to cover the full cost of OLN324’s Phase III development.

In return, Blackstone will be eligible for regulatory and commercial milestone payments, as well as royalties in the single-digit percentage range.

The funding arrangement allows J&J to advance the clinical programme while sharing development costs and financial risk with an external investment partner.

It also reflects the growing role of specialist life sciences investors in financing late-stage drug development.

J&J expands dealmaking activity

The Ollin transaction follows a series of investments and acquisitions through which J&J has strengthened its pharmaceutical pipeline.

In June, the company agreed to acquire oncology-focused Firefly Bio for US$1 billion.

A month later, its investment in Sail Biomedicines secured acquisition rights for the cell therapy specialist’s CAR-T platform.

The latest acquisition extends J&J’s business development activity into ophthalmology, adding a late-stage candidate targeting two significant retinal conditions.
